topic: How dense a neutron star is
hook: A sugar cube of this star's material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
on_screen_hook: A sugar cube weighing a *billion* tons

blocks.narration: A sugar cube of this star's material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth. It is called a neutron star.
blocks.visual: Cinematic 3D render of a tiny glowing cube resting on a scale that crushes the ground beneath it, deep blacks

blocks.narration: Neutron stars are born when a massive star runs out of fuel and its core collapses in a supernova explosion.
blocks.visual: A giant star swells, then collapses inward and erupts in a brilliant explosion

blocks.narration: The core gets crushed so hard that protons and electrons merge into neutrons, packed together tighter than atoms normally allow.
blocks.visual: Glowing particles squeeze together into a dense shimmering lattice

blocks.narration: The result packs more mass than our Sun into a sphere roughly the size of a city, about twenty kilometers across.
blocks.visual: A tiny bright sphere hovers over a city skyline for scale, dwarfed by nothing

blocks.narration: That is why a sugar cube sized piece would weigh around a billion tons. Its gravity is fierce enough to bend light around it.
blocks.visual: Starlight curves around the dense sphere like ripples around a stone

blocks.narration: Many neutron stars spin incredibly fast. Some rotate hundreds of times every second, sweeping beams of radiation through space.
blocks.visual: The star spins rapidly, twin beams sweeping like a cosmic lighthouse

blocks.narration: When those beams sweep past Earth, astronomers detect them as incredibly regular pulses, like a ticking clock. These are called pulsars.
blocks.visual: A radio telescope dish on Earth picks up rhythmic flashing signals

blocks.narration: They are some of the most extreme objects in the universe. Comment the space object you want explained next.
blocks.visual: The pulsar glows quietly in deep space as the camera pulls back

captions.body: Neutron stars pack more mass than the Sun into a sphere roughly the size of a city. NASA notes that a sugar-cube-sized amount of neutron star material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth, and some spin hundreds of times per second.
